In [[mathematics]], '''cylinder set measure''' (or '''promeasure''', or '''premeasure''', or '''quasi-measure''', or '''CSM''') is a kind of prototype for a [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] on an infinite-dimensional [[vector space]]. An example is the [[Gauss]]ian cylinder set measure on [[Hilbert space]].

Cylinder set measures are in general '''not''' measures (and in particular need not be [[Sigma additivity|countably additive]] but only [[Sigma additivity|finitely additive]]), but can be used to define  measures, such as the [[Classical Wiener space#Classical Wiener measure|classical Wiener measure]] on the set of continuous paths starting at the origin in [[Euclidean space]]. This is done in the construction of the [[abstract Wiener space]] where one defines a cylinder set Gaussian measure on a separable Hilbert space and chooses a Banach space in such a way that the cylindrical measure becomes σ-additive on the cylindrical algebra.

The terminology is not always consistent in the literature. Some authors call cylinder set measures just '''cylinder measure''' or '''cylindrical measures''' (see e.g.<ref name="Bogachev">{{cite book |first1=Vladimir |last1=Bogachev| publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|title=Gaussian Measures|place=Rhode Island|date=1998}}</ref><ref name="VaTaCho">{{cite book |title=Probability Distributions on Banach Spaces |author=N. Vakhania, V. Tarieladze and S. Chobanyan|isbn=9789027724960|lccn=87004931 |series=Mathematics and its Applications| year=1987 | publisher=Springer Netherlands |page=390}}</ref><ref>{{cite book| title=Measure and Integration Theory on Infinite-Dimensional Spaces: Abstract Harmonic Analysis | first1=Dao-Xing |last1=Xia |first2=Elmer J. |last2=Brody |place=Ukraine |publisher=Academic Press |date=1972}}</ref>), while some reserve this word only for σ-additive measures.

==Definition==
There are two equivalent ways to define a cylinder set measure.

One way is to define it directly as a set function on the [[Cylindrical σ-algebra|cylindrical algebra]] such that certain restrictions on smaller σ-algebras are σ-additive measure. This can also be expressed in terms of a finite-dimensional linear operator.

Denote by <math>\mathcal{Cyl}(N,M)</math> the cylindrical algebra defined for two spaces with [[Dual system|dual pairing]] <math>\langle,\rangle:=\langle,\rangle_{N,M}</math>, i.e. the set of all cylindrical sets
:<math>C_{f_1,\dots,f_m,B}=\{x\in N\colon (\langle x,f_1\rangle,\dots,\langle x,f_m\rangle)\in B\}</math>
for some <math>f_1,\dots,f_m\in M</math> and <math>B\in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^m)</math>.<ref>{{cite book |title=Probability Distributions on Banach Spaces |author=N. Vakhania, V. Tarieladze and S. Chobanyan|isbn=9789027724960|lccn=87004931 |series=Mathematics and its Applications| year=1987 | publisher=Springer Netherlands |page=4}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Topological Vector Spaces and Their Applications |first1=Vladimir Igorevich|last1=Bogachev |first2=Oleg Georgievich|last2=Smolyanov| isbn=978-3-319-57116-4 | doi=10.1007/978-3-319-57117-1 |series=Springer Monographs in Mathematics| year=2017| publisher=Springer Cham |page=327-333 }}</ref> This is an algebra which can also be written as the union of smaller σ-algebras.

=== Definition on the cylindrical algebra ===
Let <math>X</math> be a [[topological vector space]] over <math>\R</math>, denote its algebraic dual as <math>X^*</math> and let <math>G\subseteq X^*</math> be a subspace. Then the set function <math>\mu:\mathcal{Cyl}(X,G)\to \R_{+}</math>
is a '''cylinder set measure''' (or '''cylinderical measure''') if for any finite set <math>F=\{f_1,\dots,f_n\}\subset G</math> the restriction to 
:<math>\mu:\sigma(\mathcal{Cyl}(X,F))\to \R_{+}</math>
is a σ-additive measure. Notice that <math>\sigma(\mathcal{Cyl}(X,F))</math> is a σ-algebra while <math>\mathcal{Cyl}(X,G)</math> is not.<ref name="Bogachev" /><ref name="VaTaCho" /><ref>{{cite journal |title=Measures on linear topological spaces |first1=Oleg Georgievich|last1=Smolyanov |first2=Sergei Vasilyevich|last2=Fomin |author-link2=Sergei Fomin |journal=Russian Math. Surveys |volume=31 |number=4 |date=1976 |pages=12 |doi=10.1070/RM1976v031n04ABEH001553|bibcode=1976RuMaS..31....1S }}</ref>

As usual if <math>\mu(X)=1</math> we call it a '''cylindrical probability measure'''.

=== Operatic definition ===
Let <math>E</math> be a [[Real number|real]] [[topological vector space]]. Let <math>\mathcal{A} (E)</math> denote the collection of all [[Surjection|surjective]] [[continuous linear map]]s <math>T : E \to F_T</math> defined on <math>E</math> whose image is some finite-dimensional real vector space <math>F_T</math>:
<math display=block>\mathcal{A} (E) := \left\{ T \in \mathrm{Lin} (E; F_{T}) : T \mbox{ surjective and } \dim_{\R} F_{T} < + \infty\right\}.</math>

A '''cylinder set measure''' on <math>E</math> is a collection of [[Measure (mathematics)|measures]]
<math display=block>\left\{\mu_{T} : T \in \mathcal{A} (E)\right\}.</math>

where <math>\mu_T</math> is a measure on <math>F_T.</math> These measures are required to satisfy the following consistency condition: if <math>\pi_{ST} : F_S \to F_T</math> is a surjective [[Projection (mathematics)|projection]], then the [[pushforward measure|push forward]] of the measure is as follows:
<math display=block>\mu_{T} = \left(\pi_{ST}\right)_{*} \left(\mu_{S}\right).</math>

If <math>\mu(E)=1</math> then it's a '''cylindrical probability measure'''. Some authors define cylindrical measures explicitly as probability measures, however they don't need to be.

==Connection to the abstract Wiener spaces==
{{Main|abstract Wiener space}}
Let <math>(H,B,i)</math> be an [[abstract Wiener space]] in its classical definition by [[Leonard Gross]]. This is a separable [[Hilbert space]] <math>H</math>, a separable Banach space <math>B</math> that is the completion under a ''measurable norm'' or ''Gross-measurable norm'' <math>\|\cdot\|_1</math> and a continuous linear embedding <math>i:H\to B</math> with dense range. Gross then showed that this construction allows to continue a cylindrical Gaussian measure as a σ-additive measure on the Banach space. More precisely let <math>H'</math> be the topological dual space of <math>H</math>, he showed that a cylindrical Gaussian measure on <math>H</math> defined on the cylindrical algebra <math>\mathcal{Cyl}(H,H')</math> will be σ-additive on the cylindrical algebra <math>\mathcal{Cyl}(B,B')</math> of the Banach space. Hence the measure is also σ-additive on the cylindrical σ-algebra <math>\mathcal{E}(B,B'):=\sigma(\mathcal{Cyl}(B,B')).</math> This follows from the [[Carathéodory's extension theorem]], and is therefore also a measure in the classical sense.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Leonard |last=Gross |publisher=University of California Press |title=Abstract Wiener spaces |journal=Proceedings of the Fifth Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability |volume=Band 2: ''Contributions to Probability Theory'', Part 1 |date=1967 |pages=35}}</ref>

==Remarks==

The consistency condition
<math display=block>\mu_{T} = \left(\pi_{ST}\right)_{*} (\mu_{S})</math>
is modelled on the way that true measures push forward (see the section [[#Cylinder set measures versus true measures|cylinder set measures versus true measures]]). However, it is important to understand that in the case of cylinder set measures, this is a requirement that is part of the definition, not a result.

A cylinder set measure can be intuitively understood as defining a finitely additive function on the [[cylinder set]]s of the topological vector space <math>E.</math> The '''cylinder sets''' are the [[pre-image]]s in <math>E</math> of measurable sets in <math>F_T</math>: if <math>\mathcal{B}_{T}</math> denotes the [[σ-algebra|<math>\sigma</math>-algebra]] on <math>F_T</math> on which <math>\mu_T</math> is defined, then
<math display=block>\mathrm{Cyl} (E) := \left\{T^{-1} (B) : B \in \mathcal{B}_{T}, T \in \mathcal{A} (E)\right\}.</math>

In practice, one often takes <math>\mathcal{B}_{T}</math> to be the [[Borel sigma algebra|Borel <math>\sigma</math>-algebra]] on <math>F_T.</math> In this case, one can show that when <math>E</math> is a [[Separable space|separable]] [[Banach space]], the &sigma;-algebra generated by the cylinder sets is precisely the Borel <math>\sigma</math>-algebra of <math>E</math>:
<math display=block>\mathrm{Borel} (E) = \sigma \left(\mathrm{Cyl} (E)\right).</math>

==Cylinder set measures versus true measures==

A cylinder set measure on <math>E</math> is not actually a true measure on <math>E</math>: it is a collection of measures defined on all finite-dimensional images of <math>E.</math> If <math>E</math> has a probability measure <math>\mu</math> already defined on it, then <math>\mu</math> gives rise to a cylinder set measure on <math>E</math> using the push forward: set <math>\mu_T = T_{*}(\mu)</math>on <math>F_T.</math>

When there is a measure <math>\mu</math> on <math>E</math> such that <math>\mu_T = T_{*}(\mu)</math> in this way, it is customary to [[Abuse of notation|abuse notation]] slightly and say that the cylinder set measure <math>\left\{\mu_{T} : T \in \mathcal{A} (E)\right\}</math> "is" the measure <math>\mu.</math>

==Cylinder set measures on Hilbert spaces==

When the Banach space <math>E</math> is also a [[Hilbert space]] <math>H,</math> there is a '''{{visible anchor|canonical Gaussian cylinder set measure}}''' <math>\gamma^H</math> arising from the [[inner product]] structure on <math>H.</math> Specifically, if <math>\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle</math> denotes the inner product on <math>H,</math> let <math>\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_T</math> denote the [[quotient inner product]] on <math>F_T.</math> The measure <math>\gamma_T^H</math> on <math>F_T</math> is then defined to be the canonical [[Gaussian measure]] on <math>F_T</math>:
<math display=block>\gamma_{T}^{H} := i_{*} \left(\gamma^{\dim F_{T}}\right),</math>
where <math>i : \R^{\dim(F_T)} \to F_T</math> is an [[isometry]] of Hilbert spaces taking the [[Euclidean geometry|Euclidean]] inner product on <math>\R^{\dim(F_T)}</math> to the inner product <math>\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_T</math> on <math>F_T,</math> and <math>\gamma^n</math> is the standard [[Gaussian measure]] on <math>\R^n.</math>

The canonical Gaussian cylinder set measure on an infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space <math>H</math> does not correspond to a true measure on <math>H.</math> The proof is quite simple: the ball of radius <math>r</math> (and center 0) has measure at most equal to that of the ball of radius <math>r</math> in an <math>n</math>-dimensional Hilbert space, and this tends to 0 as <math>n</math> tends to infinity. So the ball of radius <math>r</math> has measure 0; as the Hilbert space is a countable union of such balls it also has measure 0, which is a contradiction. (See [[Infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure|infinite dimensional Lebesgue measure]].)

An alternative proof that the Gaussian cylinder set measure is not a measure uses the [[Cameron–Martin theorem]] and a result on the [[Quasi-invariant measure|quasi-invariance of measures]]. If <math>\gamma^H = \gamma</math> really were a measure, then the [[identity function]] on <math>H</math> would [[radonify]] that measure, thus making <math>\operatorname{id} : H \to H</math> into an [[abstract Wiener space]]. By the Cameron–Martin theorem, <math>\gamma</math> would then be quasi-invariant under translation by any element of <math>H,</math> which implies that either <math>H</math> is finite-dimensional or that <math>\gamma</math> is the zero measure. In either case, we have a contradiction.

[[Sazonov's theorem]] gives conditions under which the [[Pushforward measure|push forward]] of a canonical Gaussian cylinder set measure can be turned into a true measure.

==Nuclear spaces and cylinder set measures==

A cylinder set measure on the dual of a [[Nuclear space|nuclear]] [[Fréchet space]] automatically extends to a measure if its Fourier transform is continuous.

'''Example''': Let <math>S</math> be the space of [[Distribution (mathematics)|Schwartz function]]s on a finite dimensional vector space; it is nuclear. It is contained in the Hilbert space <math>H</math> of [[Lp space|<math>L^2</math> functions]], which is in turn contained in the space of [[Tempered representation|tempered distributions]] <math>S^\prime,</math> the dual of the [[Nuclear space|nuclear]] [[Fréchet space]] <math>S</math>:
<math display=block>S \subseteq H \subseteq S^\prime.</math>

The Gaussian cylinder set measure on <math>H</math> gives a cylinder set measure on the space of tempered distributions, which extends to a measure on the space of tempered distributions, <math>S^\prime.</math>

The Hilbert space <math>H</math> has measure 0 in <math>S^\prime,</math> by the first argument used above to show that the canonical Gaussian cylinder set measure on <math>H</math> does not extend to a measure on <math>H.</math>
